paper_summary: Persian-language study (Loghman et al., Advanced Materials in Engineering 43(1), 2024) on vinyl ester / hollow glass microballoon syntactic foams. Pure VE-200 vinyl ester resin and foams with 20, 40 and 60 vol% silane-treated H38H glass microballoons (true density 0.38 g/cm3) were cast in silicone moulds, cured at room temperature and post-cured at 80 C for 3 h. Density fell from 1.04 to 0.56 g/cm3 while compressive strength fell from 80 to 55 MPa and tensile strength from 45 to 17 MPa; specific compressive strength rose from 76.9 to 98.2 MPa.cm3/g. Results are compared in Table 6 with Gupta et al. (Compos. B Eng. 2010) vinyl ester foams made with 0.32 g/cm3 microballoons.

extraction_notes: PAPER IS IN PERSIAN; the PDF text layer is right-to-left reversed, so Persian decimal numbers appear as '04 /1' meaning 1.04 and '15 /0±' meaning +/-0.15. All decodings were cross-checked arithmetically: Table 6 modulus/density = Table 6 specific modulus, and Table 6 strength/Table 5 density = Table 5 specific strength, and they agree to rounding for every present-study row, which confirms the column mapping. UNITS: GPa moduli from Table 6 converted to MPa (x1000); specific moduli converted from GPa.cm3/g to MPa.cm3/g (x1000). Vol% converted to fractions. CAVEATS: (1) The abstract states the highest tensile strength (neat resin) is 40 MPa while Table 6 lists 45 +/- 2.9 MPa; the table value was used since it is internally consistent with the Table 5 specific tensile strength of 43.2 MPa.cm3/g. (2) Table 5's 'theoretical density' column (0.878/0.784/0.690/0.596 g/cm3) is lower than the measured density for the 0, 20 and 40 vol% samples, so the paper's void formula (rho_T - rho_ex)/rho_T yields NEGATIVE porosity for those three rows even though the table prints the magnitudes 18.4%, 12.2% and 1.4%. The theoretical densities are recorded as printed, but matrix_porosity_fraction is left null for 0/20/40 vol% and only recorded (0.0604) for the 60 vol% sample where the value is genuinely positive. A theoretical density of 0.878 g/cm3 for neat vinyl ester is also inconsistent with the stated resin density of 1.13 g/cm3 (Table 3), so this column looks unreliable. (3) Table 5 also contains three columns of Gupta-group data (specific compressive strength 73.0/80.3/83.0/85.1 MPa.cm3/g, matrix void 4.4/7.3/6.8/8.9%, density 0.869/0.765/0.690/0.597 g/cm3), but those rows cannot be aligned unambiguously with the Gupta compositions (30/40/50/60 vol%) listed in Table 6 - the products do not reproduce the Table 6 strengths - so they were NOT attached to the secondary records. (4) Gupta secondary rows from Table 6 are also internally inconsistent (modulus / specific modulus implies densities of ~0.91, 0.85, 0.81/0.71, 0.91/0.80 g/cm3 for compression vs tension), and the tensile strengths of 8 and 7 MPa at 50 and 60 vol% may be OCR-truncated; these records were given low extractor_confidence. (5) Batch masses are 100 g resin + 0/10/22/40 g microballoons (Table 4); particle_weight_fraction was left null because the catalyst/accelerator masses are given only as volumes so an exact weight fraction cannot be formed. (6) Strain rate was not stated; only the crosshead rate of 1 mm/min (0.1 mm/min in the cited Gupta work) is given, so strain_rate_per_s is null and the crosshead rate is recorded in specimen_notes. Test temperature is never stated, so temperature_c is null. (7) Plateau stress, energy absorption, densification strain and strain at failure appear only in the stress-strain plots of Figs. 5 and 7 with no numeric values in text or tables, so they are left null. (8) Particle mean diameter 45 um is the D50 from Table 1 (D90 = 85 um); Table 1 also gives a microballoon crush strength of 31 MPa and a density range of 0.36-0.40 g/cm3 around the nominal 0.38 g/cm3.
